raw_response:
I've been farming these 225 mu for 15 years now — started when I was about 27, took over from my father and kept expanding bit by bit. I'm in my early 40s. Middle school education, which around here means I can read pesticide labels and understand what the extension technician tells me, but I still trust my own eyes more than any book.

My household has four people: my wife, our two kids, and me. The kids help during summer vacation but they're in school most of the year, so for a farm this size I hire workers. I've got two tractors and a combine, and I use machinery for the wheat-maize fields, but chili and stevia need too much hand work for machines.

**Wheat (160 mu):** The wheat-maize double crop is my bread and butter — it's on my best flat land with good well water. Last year I got about 480 kg/mu on this ground with 18 kg nitrogen. The soil still looks pretty good after the summer rains, so I'm sticking with an improved wheat variety, planting around October 15th. I'm going with 19 kg N/mu this year — fertilizer price is a bit lower than last spring, so I can afford to push it slightly without hurting my cash flow. I'll do three fertilizer applications: compound fertilizer as base at planting, then urea topdress at green-up and again at jointing. I'll irrigate four times — planting water, green-up, jointing, and grain filling. My neighbor Lao Wang has similar land and he irrigates four times; three times cost less but last dry spring his yield dropped 40 kg/mu, and I can't afford that on 160 mu. I'll spray herbicide once and fungicide once if it looks humid in spring.

**Maize (160 mu, same land):** The turnaround after wheat harvest is brutal — sometimes only 3 days. I'll plant hybrid maize around June 14th right after the combine finishes. Minimal tillage, just light cultivation and go. I'll put down compound fertilizer at planting and topdress urea once at jointing in July — total about 17 kg N/mu. Maize needs less fuss than wheat. I'll irrigate twice if July is dry; if we get good rains, maybe only once. Herbicide at planting, and I'll watch for corn borer — if I see moths in late July, I'll spray insecticide.

**Chili (40 mu):** I started chili five years ago after seeing Old Zhang in the next village make good money. It's risky — prices swing — but when it works, profit per mu beats wheat-maize. I use plastic mulch to save water and keep weeds down. Transplant in late April. More fertilizer than wheat, especially potassium — 16 kg N, 7 kg P, 6 kg K per mu, side-dressed at flowering and fruiting. Six irrigations, lots of pesticide (herbicide, insecticide, fungicide all needed), and heavy labor. I'll hire 8–10 workers for the multiple picks from July to October. I'm targeting 320 kg/mu of dry chili, but honestly if I get 280 kg/mu and price stays above 12 yuan/kg, I'm happy.

**Stevia (25 mu):** This is my newest crop — started three years ago after a buyer from Shandong set up a collection point in the county. Contract price is stable at 8 yuan/kg dry leaf, which is why I keep it even though harvest is labor-intensive. Plant in mid-May, harvest late September. I use raised beds and fine seedbed prep. Lower fertilizer than the others — 12 kg N, 5 kg P, 4 kg K — stevia doesn't like too much nitrogen or the glycoside content drops. Five irrigations, hand weeding mostly under the mulch. I'll hire workers for harvesting; the leaves have to be picked before frost.

**Cash and tradeoffs:** Total input costs will run about 125,000 yuan this year. That's a lot, but as a business farm I have cash reserves from last year. I thought about expanding chili to 60 mu, but that would mean less wheat-maize, and wheat-maize is my insurance — even in a bad year I still have grain to sell and straw for feed. Stevia is only 25 mu because the buyer's contract caps how much he'll take from me. Labor is my biggest constraint in June and September — wheat harvest, maize planting, and stevia harvest all overlap, so I have to line up workers two weeks ahead and pay a bit extra to guarantee they'll show up.
